1:
Four of them begin by pairing the psalm with the one before it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the alphabetical psalm which celebrated the government of God is followed by another of identical structure, twenty-two lines as an old version correctly counts, which celebrates the men whose conduct is ordered after the divine pattern; what was there said of the righteousness of God is here said of the righteousness of the man who fears him, since that righteousness is the copy of the divine and is by nature love. John Calvin notes the same acrostic form and adds that since the subject is only an enlargement of the last verse of the preceding psalm, it is not improbable that one author composed both. Adam Clarke counts the letters exactly and reports that the psalm is understood to have been written after the captivity and is ascribed by the old Latin version to two of the prophets of the Return. Augustine of Hippo had that ascription in his title and made something of it: those prophets were not yet in existence when the verses were sung, yet both began to prophesy the restoration of the temple, so that whoever turns himself to the work of that building understands the title.

What righteousness it is that endures divides them along an unexpected line. Charles Ellicott holds that the parallel in the ninth verse, where the same clause returns, requires the limited sense the rabbinical writings give the word, namely liberality or beneficence, while granting that the saying is true in its widest sense. Adam Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the words themselves, since both the Hebrew and the Greek are often used not only of justice but of beneficence and almsgiving, and this is most probably the meaning here. John Wesley makes it rather the fruit or reward of righteousness, that is, God’s blessing upon the man’s estate. John Gill turns the wealth of the same verse into the unsearchable riches of Christ and the durable riches that go with an everlasting righteousness. Adam Clarke elsewhere gives the plainest account of how the wealth is come by, that a converted man saves both the time and the money he formerly squandered, and warns that if he does not distribute to the poor his savings will become a curse or be swept away by providence.

Whose graciousness the fourth verse describes is disputed. Charles Ellicott says the received version is right in making the words a description of the upright man’s character, and meets the objection that the construction is strange, since the upright stands in the plural while the epithets resume the singular; his explanation is that the first clause is a familiar proverbial saying which the poet quotes without altering its number to suit his own sentence. Keil and Delitzsch report a rival construction which ties the epithets to the upright as a relative clause and pronounce it impossible. Matthew Henry notices what makes the verse remarkable: the same words were said of God in the psalm before and are here said of the good man, for herein we must be followers of God as dear children. Adam Clarke traces the sequence, that the man enjoys the favour of God, that grace makes him compassionate, and that the compassion issues in giving to the really poor and lending to those who need only present help; but he adds that the good man takes heed both to whom he gives and to whom he lends, that his bounty may be well applied and that he may not oblige one who under the notion of a loan means to keep the money. C.H. Spurgeon keeps to the first verse and distinguishes a slavish fear which is accursed from a godly fear sweetened into filial love, in which holiness is the man’s happiness and truth his treasure.
5:
The opening verse is rendered by Charles Ellicott in a way that changes both its halves. The word we translate good, he says, is not used here in a moral sense but means prosperous, so that the line runs, happy is the man who gives and lends; and the clause about guiding affairs with discretion he would render that the man will gain his cause in the judgment, which is apparently how the old Greek and Latin took it, though others render that he will sustain his affairs by justice, the verb meaning primarily to measure and in this form to sustain. He adds that the parallel in the following verse confirms the sense. John Gill reaches half of the same point from usage, since a good man here is not only one who has the good work of grace in him but one who is munificent, bountiful and liberal, a sense the word bears in Latin writers as well. John Wesley keeps the received clause and defines the discretion negatively, as not getting an estate unjustly, nor casting it away prodigally, nor yet withholding it from those who need it.

Why the man is not moved is answered at different depths. John Gill makes it a doctrine of perseverance: he shall not be moved out of the heart of God, nor out of the covenant, nor off the foundation, and though he may be so shaken as to fall into sin he shall not perish everlastingly. John Wesley puts the same more briefly, that though afflicted for a season he shall not be eternally destroyed. Matthew Henry divides the stability into a settled reputation and a settled spirit, and finds the second the greater satisfaction, since a man may then rejoice in himself alone and not in another; on the first he observes that those who are forgotten on earth and despised are remembered and honoured elsewhere. He then defines the charity that earns the remembrance in a sentence that bears on the whole psalm: alms are called righteousness not because they justify us by making atonement for our evil deeds, but because they are good deeds which we are bound to perform, so that if we are not charitable we are not just, since we withhold good from those to whom it is due.

Why evil tidings do not frighten him is illustrated by one and explained by the others. Charles Ellicott points to the sufferer whose messengers of ill succeeded one another so fast that the story has become the standing instance, and adds that a good conscience before God is the best armour against fate, quoting a dramatist for the saying that virtue is bold and goodness never fearful. Adam Clarke gives the reason rather than the instance: the man knows that God governs the world and therefore does not fear for the future, and as to the calumnies of men he does not fear them because his heart is fixed to walk in the path of duty whatever persecutions follow. John Gill divides the tidings, temporal ones such as the death of friends and the convulsions of nations, and spiritual ones brought by the adversary or by an unbelieving heart, or an ill report raised against the man himself; and he extends them to what shall befall the churches in the latter day, since the man knows that the saints will be carried through it. John Wesley keeps to the report of approaching calamities.
8:
The established heart is described physically by one and doctrinally by another. Adam Clarke renders that the man’s heart is propped up, buttressed by the strength of his Maker. John Gill makes the establishment doctrinal, a heart nourished and strengthened by the teaching of grace and settled in the faith, so that the man is not as a child tossed to and fro with every wind. The scattering that follows is read the same way by all of them but measured differently. John Gill takes it of one who scatters as a sower scatters seed, not throwing all in one place but some here and some there. Charles Ellicott observes that the form of the verb indicates a frequent and customary action rather than a single act, and refers to the apostle who quotes the verse. Adam Clarke says plainly that the righteousness which remains for ever here is the man’s almsgiving, and adds of the exalted horn that he rises to influence only through his own worth and not by extortion or flattery. John Wesley gives the sharpest form of the same thought: what a man gives is not lost, but is indeed the only part of his estate which will abide with him to all eternity.

Who it is that sees and is grieved turns on a number. Adam Clarke notes that the word stands in the singular and that some think the adversary himself is meant, since it is distinguished from the wicked in the plural at the close of the same verse. John Gill and C.H. Spurgeon both keep to ungodly men, Gill applying the sight to the enemies who must behold the vindication of those they opposed, and Spurgeon observing that the child of wrath is obliged to witness the blessedness of the righteous though the sight makes him gnaw his own heart. C.H. Spurgeon presses the figures: the man would gladly grind the righteous between his teeth, and since he cannot he grinds his teeth against each other; and a life that melts as it proceeds, leaving a slimy trail behind it like a snail, is a horrible thing. Charles Ellicott glosses the same verb as we do when we speak of consuming with vexation. John Wesley divides the desire that perishes between the wish for the misery of good men and the wish for one’s own unbroken prosperity, and C.H. Spurgeon adds that the very wickedness by which the man hoped to accomplish his purpose shall be his defeat.
